2. Remarks/Discussion of Issues
Claims
By the present Amendment, claim 18 has been canceled, without prejudice and without disclaimer of the subject matter. Claims 16, 17, 20, 21, 24-27, 29 and 30 have been revised. Claims 16-17 and 19-33 are pending in the application, which Applicant respectfully submits are in condition for allowance.
To the extent the Examiner believes there is not a clear basis for entry of the present amendment, Applicant respectfully requests consideration of the amendment under the AFCP 2.0 Program, and submit herewith Form PTO/SB/434 in support of the request.
35 U.S.C. § 101 Rejection
The Office Action rejects claims 16-26 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as assertedly being directed to non-statutory subject mater. See Office Action, p. 2-3. The Office Action asserts that the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea), and that the claims do not include additional elements that integrate the abstract ideal into a practical application, or amount to significantly more than the abstract idea. Id. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.
According to the United States Supreme Court in Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int'l, 573 U.S. 208, 134 S. Ct. 2347, 110 USPQ2d 1976 (2014), the determination of whether a claim is directed to patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 comprises a two-part analysis. First, it must be determined whether the claim is directed to a "patent-ineligible concept" (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, or physical phenomena). Second, if the claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept, it must be determined whether "an element or combination of elements that is 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself."' See, e.g., Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357, 110 USPQ2d at 1981.
The 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, United States Patent and Trademark Office (December 16, 2014), provides a two-part analysis, after an initial step of determining whether the claim is directed to a processes, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, regarding how the Office determines whether a claim is directed toward section 101 patent-eligible subject matter. Interim Eligibility Guidance, Federal Register/Vol. 79, No. 241/Tuesday, December 16, 2014/Rules and Regulations, p. 74621. Thus, after first determining the first step (Step 1) of whether the claim is to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, one must perform the two part Alice analysis: (A) Determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A), and (B) if an abstract idea is present in the claim, determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself (Step 2B). See also MPEP 2106(III).
With regard to Step 1, under 35 U.S.C. § 101, there are four categories of subject matter eligible for patent protection: (1) processes; (2) machines; (3) manufactures; and (4) compositions of matter. Claims 16-23 and 26 are directed to machines or manufactures, and claims 24 and 25 are directed to processes, and therefore all claims fall within 35 U.S.C. § 101.
Step 2A addresses whether the method and article of manufacture are directed to an abstract idea. Notably, claims should not be deemed as being directed to an abstract idea simply because they are implemented using a computer. See, e.g., McRO, Inc. v.
Bandai Namco Games America Inc., 837 F.3d 1299, 1303 (Fed Cir. 2016) (Federal Circuit disposes of the general notion that computer implementation of a process is automatically a non-statutory, abstract idea, holding "that the ordered combination of claimed steps, using unconventional rules that relate sub-sequences of phonemes, timings, and morph weight sets, is not directed to an abstract idea and is therefore patent- eligible subject matter under § 101.").
According to the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, Step 2A is further divided into two prongs for determining whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception, including abstract ideas. In Prong One, it is determined whether the claim recites a judicial exception, and with regard to an abstract idea in particular, whether the claim recites subject matter from one of three groupings: (a) mathematical concepts, (b) certain methods of organizing human activity-fundamental economic principles or practices, and (c) mental processes. "Claims that do not recite matter that falls within these enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas ...." See Federal Register / Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 53. If it is determined that the claim does recite a judicial exception, then the analysis proceeds to Prong Two of Step 2A. In Prong Two, it is determined whether the recited judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea) is integrated into a practical application of that judicial exception. Id.
With regard to Prong One, the revised guidance for analyzing patentable subject matter provides: "Claims do not recite a mental process when they do not contain limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind, for instance when the human mind is not equipped to perform the claim limitations. See SRIInt'l, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 930 F.3d 1295, 1304 (Fed. Cir. 2019) (declining to identify the claimed collection and analysis of network data as abstract because 'the human mind is not equipped to detect suspicious activity by using network monitors and analyzing network packets as recited by the claims')..." See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(III)(A) (emphasis added).
Similarly, claim 16, for example, is directed to a catheter for being introduced into the cavity, wherein the catheter is shape sensing enabled. Claim 16 also recites and a memory storing instructions causing a computer determine whether the bendable segment is in contact with an inner wall of the cavity; determine at least one contact curve defined by the bendable segment in each arrangement of the bendable segment determined to be in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, and determine at least one non-contact curve defined by the bendable segment in each arrangement of the bendable segment determined not to be in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, using shape sensing information from the catheter, none of which can be performed in the human mind.
Likewise, reconstructing the cavity, in response to the determined at least one contact curve and the at least one non-contact curve, to provide a map for guiding the catheter, cannot be performed in the human mind. Applicant therefore respectfully submits that claim 16 is not directed to an abstract idea.
However, assuming arguendo that claim 16, recites at least one abstract idea, the question becomes whether that abstract idea is integrated into a practical application. "A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception." See Federal Register/Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 54 (emphasis added).
In the present Application, claim 16 integrates any potential abstract idea into at least the practical application of reconstructing the cavity, in response to the determined at least one contact curve and the at least one non-contact curve, to provide a map for guiding the catheter. This practical limitation prevents monopolization (improper pre- emption) of any potential abstract idea recited in claim 16, and therefore evidences a practical application of the same.
Another consideration indicative of an additional element integrating the judicial exception into a practical application is whether it reflects an improvement in the function of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or technical field. Id. In this context, the claimed embodiments result in improvements in the field of medical imaging, where a cavity (e.g., heart) can be more quickly and effectively reconstructed using set of curves defined by a bendable segment of a catheter, as opposed to relying on points of contact by the distal tip of the catheter.
The Specification identifies the technical problem addressed by the claimed subject matter as: "Since in an acceptable time only few different positions of the tip of the ablation catheter within the cavity can be determined, the reconstructed cavity, which is determined based on only these few locations of the tip of the ablation catheter, has a poor quality only." See Specification, p. 1, lines 14-17.
The claimed subject matter provides an improvement in the technical field that addresses this technical problem: "It is an object of the present invention to provide a cavity determination apparatus, a cavity determination method and a cavity determination computer program for determining a cavity within an object, which allows determining the cavity within the object with improved quality in a relatively short time." See p. 1, lines 20-23 (emphasis added). In more detail:
The apparatus described above with reference to Figs. 1 and 2 is therefore preferentially adapted such that the positioning device can be replaced by a shape sensing device, which enables the reconstruction to be based on curves, rather than points, in a much faster fashion. In particular, shape sensing technology is preferentially used, in order to recover very quickly the shape of the cavity.... In particular, a catheter may be moved rapidly and in a more or less random fashion to quickly get the bulk of the cavity, for instance, of the left atrium of a heart of a person. The outcome of the corresponding algorithm can then be used as a rough map to guide the catheter into areas where the acquisition should be refined, for instance, because of a particularly high interest in this area and/or because the area is more difficult to access due to larger curvatures which could have hampered a correct acquisition during the initial sweep. Higher curvatures may be present, for instance, in pulmonary veins.
See p. 12, line 27 - p. 13, line 6 (emphasis added). See also p. 2, lines 1-13 ("Since not only single locations within the cavity are acquired, but curves defined by the bendable segment within the cavity in the different arrangements, a lot of spatial information can be acquired very fast. This allows reconstructing the cavity with improved quality in a relatively short time.") (emphasis added); p. 6, lines 3-7 ("The introduction element and the curve determination unit are preferentially adapted to determine the curves defined by the bendable segment within the cavity by optical shape sensing. This allows the apparatus to reliably determine the different curves defined by the bendable segment within the cavity, without necessarily requiring further localization units like an electromagnetic localization unit or an x-ray localization unit.") (emphasis added). Thus, claim 16 clearly is directed to improvements in other technology or technical field.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the claims also satisfy Prong Two in Step 2A of the analysis as set forth 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance. Therefore, the first part of the Alice analysis is satisfied, and the second part need not be addressed.
However, assuming arguendo that Step 2A has not been satisfied, Applicant proceeds to apply the second part of the Alice analysis (Step 2B). In accordance with Step 2B, Applicant submits that various elements in the claims are sufficient to ensure that the claims amount to significantly more than the abstract idea itself, particularly in that the claims as a whole is for a particular application of the asserted abstract idea. See, e.g., Federal Register/Vol. 84, No. 4/Monday, January 7, 2019/Notices, p. 56 ("[I]f a claim has been determined to be directed to a judicial exception under revised Step 2A, examiners should then evaluate the additional elements individually and in combination under Step 2B to determine whether they provide an inventive concept (i.e., whether the additional elements amount to significantly more than the exception itself.").
For example, claim 16 recites inter alia a catheter for being introduced into the cavity, wherein the catheter is shape sensing enabled and comprises a bendable segment for being arranged within the cavity in different arrangements, and in response to determinations of contact and non-contact curves, reconstruct the cavity to provide a map for guiding the catheter.
Accordingly, even assuming elements may involve abstract ideas, the claims are still directed to patent eligible subject matter due to application of the inventive concept. Applicant submits that the claims satisfy the second stage of the Alice Corp. test, and that the claims amount to significantly more than the abstract idea itself. See, e.g. Electric Power Group, LLC v. Alstom S.A., 830 F.3d 1350 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("Reflecting those points, we have described ... the second-stage inquiry (where reached) as looking more precisely at what the claim elements add-specifically, whether, in the Supreme Court's terms, they identify an "'inventive concept"' in the application of the ineligible matter to which (by assumption at stage two) the claim is directed." (citing Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp., 822 F.3d 1327, 1335-36 (Fed. Cir. 2016); Internet Patents Corp. v.
Active Network, Inc., 790 F.3d 1343, 1346 (Fed. Cir. 2015); Bascom Global Internet Servs., Inc. v. AT&TMobilityLLC, No. 2015-1763, 2016 WL 3514158, at *5 (Fed. Cir. June 27, 2016)).
Notably, the "inventive concept" that transforms the abstract idea into a patent- eligible invention "may arise in one or more of the individual claim limitations or in the ordered combination of the limitations," as discussed above. See BASCOM, at p. 13 (citing Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2355) (emphasis added). In addition, as discussed above in the analysis under Prong Two of revised Step 2A, the claim features recite improvements in other technology or technical field. Again, such improvements amount to "significantly more" than the assertedly abstract idea itself, transforming the abstract idea into a patent- eligible application. See, e.g., Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357, 110 USPQ2d at 1981 (Syllabus at 3, Slip Op. at 15). See also BASCOM, p. 17 ("Thus, construed in favor of the nonmovant -BASCOM the claims are 'more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the [abstract idea].' Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357. Instead, the claims may be read to "improve[] an existing technological process." Id. at 2358 (discussing the claims in Diehr, 450 U.S. 175)."). Accordingly, even assuming the claims are directed to abstract ideas, they still include patent eligible subject matter since they recite improvements to a technical field in accordance with the Alice analysis.
Accordingly, for at least the reasons set forth above, Applicant respectfully submits that the second part of the Alice test is also not satisfied, and therefore respectfully request withdrawal of the rejection of all pending claims under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
35 U.S.C. §103 Rejection
Claims 16-33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Barbagli et al. (U.S. Patent No. 2009/0076476) in view of Verard et al. (U.S. Patent App. Pub. No. 2004/0097805). See Office Action, p. 4.
Claim 16
In rejecting claim 16, the Office Action asserts that "a catheter for being introduced into the cavity" is taught by catheter 604, FIGs. 1, 8-10, 17-18; that "wherein the catheter is shape sensing enabled" is taught by paras. [0008], [0060], [0079]; that "comprises a bendable segment for being arranged within the cavity in different arrangements" is taught by paras. [0055]-[0057], FIGs. 1, 8-10, 17-18; that "a computer including a non-transitory storage medium for storing instructions that, when executed by the computer, cause the computer to" is taught by position determining system 70, paras.
[0060], [0078]; and that "reconstruct the cavity [in response to the determined set of curves]" is taught by 3-D mapping system 302, paras. [0072]-[0073]. See Office Action, pp. 4-5.
The Office Action acknowledges that Barbagli et al. does expressly disclose the use of curves to make determinations, "determine a set of curves defined by the bendable segment using shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein each curve is defined by an introduction of the bendable segment within the cavity in a respective arrangement of the different arrangements, and wherein the determined set of curves comprises contact curves and non-contact curves," and "reconstruct the cavity in response to the determined set of curves," and therefore relies on Verard et al. in combination with Barbagli et al. to assertedly teach the same. See Office Action, p. 5.
In particular, the Office Action asserts that "determine a set of curves" is taught by paras. [0017], [0041], [0100]; that "defined by the bendable segment using shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein each curve is defined by an introduction of the bendable segment within the cavity in a respective arrangement of the different arrangements" is taught by paras. [0100], [0109]; and that "wherein the determined set of curves comprises contact curves and non-contact curves" is taught by paras. [0099], [0100], [0109], [0123]-[0125] of Verard et al. Id.
Without acquiescing to the grounds of rejection, and in order to further prosecution, Applicant has revised claim 16 inter alia to recite determining whether the bendable segment is in contact with an inner wall of the cavity in each arrangement of a plurality of different arrangements of the bendable segment introduced within the cavity, determining at least one contact curve defined by the bendable segment in each arrangement of the bendable segment determined to be in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, and determine at least one non-contact curve defined by the bendable segment in each arrangement of the bendable segment determined not to be in contact with the inner wall of the cavity, using shape sensing information from the catheter, and reconstructing the cavity, in response to the determined at least one contact curve and the at least one non-contact curve, to provide a map for guiding the catheter.
The Office Action relies on paras. [0100] and [0109] of Verard et al. to assertedly teach determining a set of curves defined by the bendable segment using shape sensing information from the catheter, wherein each curve is defined by an introduction of the bendable segment within the cavity in a respective arrangement of the different arrangements. The Office Action relies on paras. [0099], [0100], [0109] and [0123]- [0125] of Verard et al. to assertedly teach contact curves and non-contact curves. Para.
[0100], for example, describes providing real time feedback of "catheter curvature" to improve steering. Para. [0109] describes image 178 that includes icon 180 representing the position and location of catheter 52, as well as a curved projection 182 of the icon 180 showing where the catheter 52 will travel if it continues along its current curved trajectory. Paras. [0123]-[0125] describe different types of catheters, which may be curved, such as spiral catheters and balloon catheters.
However, there is no teaching of distinguishing between contact and non-contact curves, or specifically determining whether a bendable segment of a catheter is in contact with an inner wall of the cavity in each arrangement of different arrangements of the bendable segment introduced within the cavity. Any contact or non-contact of the catheters described by Verard et al. is incidental to positioning of the catheter, and is not considered in determining curves defined by the bendable segment in the different arrangements. Indeed, Verard et al. does not even use the word "contact" in the entire written description. It follows that there is not teaching of reconstructing the cavity, in response to the determined at least one contact curve and the at least one non-contact curve, to provide a map for guiding the catheter.
Accordingly, without acquiescing to the propriety of the proposed combination of references, Applicant respectfully submits that no proper combination of Barbagli et al. and Verard et al. teaches or suggests all the limitations of independent claim 16. Thus, the rejection of claim 16 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.
Claims 24 and 26
Without acquiescing to the propriety of the proposed combination of references, Applicant respectfully submits that no proper combination of Barbagli et al. and Verard et al. teaches or suggests all the limitations of independent claims 24 and 26 at least for substantially the same reasons set forth above with regard to claim 16. Thus, the rejection of claims 24 and 26 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.
Claims 17, 19-23, 25 and 27-33
Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection of claims 17, 19-23, 25 and 27-33, and submit that these claims are allowable over the applied art at least because they depend from independent claims 16, 24 and 26, respectively, which have been shown to be allowable, as well as in view of their additional recitations. Thus, withdrawal of the rejections of claims 17, 19-23, 25 and 27-33 is respectfully requested.
Conclusion
In view of the foregoing explanations, Applicant respectfully requests that theExaminer reconsider and reexamine the present application, allow claims 16-17 and 19-33, and pass the application to issue. In the event that there are any outstanding mattersremaining in the present application, the Examiner is invited to contact Van C. Ernest(Reg. No. 44,099) at (571) 283.0720 to discuss these matters.
